Carry out every rag, solvent drop and paper towel. Never rinse brushes in tide pools or the harbor.
Keep sidewalks, causeways and wharf edges clear. On Rocky Neck and Bearskin Neck, set up where people can walk past.
Ask before painting on private wharves or lawns, and honor 'No Trespassing' signs.
Buy your paint, panels and frames from Cape Ann shops when you can. They keep the art community here.
If people ask what you're painting, tell them. Plein-air painters have been Gloucester's ambassadors since the 1850s.

Trail · by car, with a walk on Rocky Neck

Ten stops for the women who painted Gloucester, from Fitz Henry Lane’s circle in the 1850s to Nell Blaine’s harbor in the 1950s. Most stops are outdoors and free; the museum stop is the one place to see several of their paintings at once.

In 2024 the Cape Ann Museum gathered this history in ⟦0⟧Women Artists on Cape Ann, 1870–1970⟦1⟧, curated by Martha Oaks⟦2⟧. This trail follows the places that can still be visited. Several houses on it are private homes: view them from the street and keep the sidewalk clear.
A full day. Stops 4–7 are a short walk on Rocky Neck; drive between the rest.
The map needs JavaScript. Every stop below has an address and a directions link.

A minister’s wife from Sterling, Massachusetts, Mellen came into Fitz Henry Lane’s world after her brother-in-law took the Universalist pulpit in Gloucester in 1855. By the middle of the decade she was working beside Lane, with free use of his drawings and at times his canvases; one painting, ⟦0⟧Coast of Maine⟦1⟧, carries both their signatures⟦2⟧. Her ⟦3⟧Field Beach, Stage Fort Park⟦4⟧, about 1850, shows this shore and is at the Cape Ann Museum⟦5⟧; Bowdoin owns her ⟦6⟧Gloucester Harbor (Laying Nets)⟦7⟧⟦8⟧.

The museum owns Theresa Bernstein’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester in Blue⟦1⟧ (1925)⟦2⟧, Nell Blaine’s ⟦3⟧Wharf Studio, Gloucester⟦4⟧ (1958)⟦5⟧ and the archive of the Folly Cove Designers⟦6⟧; the Rocky Neck Art Colony also credits it with Martha Walter’s ⟦7⟧Rocky Neck Store and My Studio⟦8⟧ (1920)⟦9⟧. Ask at the desk which are on view.

In the summer of 1923 Jo Nivison painted ⟦0⟧Church Towers, Gloucester⟦1⟧, a head-on view of this church’s twin towers. It was the summer she and Edward Hopper painted together here, and she encouraged him to take up watercolor⟦2⟧. We have not found the painting in a public collection.
On foot · about 1.5 km (1.0 mi) of streets

Bernstein first came to Gloucester in 1916. She and the painter William Meyerowitz stayed here after their marriage in 1919, and in 1924 bought a house on Mount Pleasant Avenue in East Gloucester (a private home), where they hosted friends including Milton Avery. Both helped found the North Shore Arts Association⟦0⟧.

A Philadelphia painter trained under William Merritt Chase, Walter had joined the Gloucester colony by 1913 and kept a studio and gallery on Rocky Neck from the later 1910s into the 1920s. The building is now a gallery⟦0⟧.
In 1924 Sally Michel rented the studio next to Milton Avery’s here. They married in 1926, and her work supported the family while he painted⟦0⟧.
Nell Blaine (1922–1996) · Rocky Neck Avenue, Gloucester · marker approximate

Blaine rented studios on Rocky Neck in 1954 and 1958⟦0⟧; the Whitney’s ⟦1⟧Harbor and Green Cloth, II⟦2⟧ dates from the second summer⟦3⟧. From 1974 until her death she summered in East Gloucester⟦4⟧. The marker is placed on the avenue; the studio addresses are not published.
Walter’s entries at the Pennsylvania Academy in 1915 included a crowded beach at Bass Rocks; Philadelphia critics praised the Gloucester picture⟦0⟧. Parking along Atlantic Road is limited.
Bernstein was still painting this beach around 1980, when she was about ninety: the Brooklyn Museum owns ⟦0⟧Rabbits, Good Harbor Beach, Gloucester⟦1⟧⟦2⟧. Summer parking is by fee.
Virginia Lee Burton (1909–1968) · Washington Street (Route 127), Lanesville

The children’s author of ⟦0⟧Mike Mulligan and His Steam Shovel⟦1⟧ taught block printing to her neighbors here and in 1941 founded the Folly Cove Designers, who printed textiles by hand until 1969⟦2⟧. Their blocks, fabrics and records are at the Cape Ann Museum⟦3⟧.

The portrait painter Cecilia Beaux (1855–1942) summered at Green Alley, her house on Eastern Point, from 1906 until her death⟦0⟧. The road is private, so the house is not a stop. Her ⟦1⟧Half-Tide, Annisquam River⟦2⟧ is in the guide.
Jane Peterson (1876–1965) painted Gloucester’s streets and wharves in bright, broken color in the 1910s and 1920s⟦0⟧. The RISD Museum owns her ⟦1⟧Gloucester Street Scene⟦2⟧⟦3⟧.

Trail · a downtown walk, then a drive

Hopper came to Gloucester in 1912 with his friend Leon Kroll, and again in the summers of 1923, 1924, 1926 and 1928, mostly painting houses in watercolor. Twelve of his subjects can still be found. The downtown walk passes eight of them and ends at the train station.

The summers are the Cape Ann Museum’s count⟦0⟧; the oil ⟦1⟧Sun on Prospect Street⟦2⟧ is dated 1934. Street addresses follow Catherine Ryan’s catalogue ⟦3⟧Edward Hopper All Around Gloucester⟦4⟧⟦5⟧, with the museum records for each painting. The Cape Ann Museum also runs docent-led “Hopper’s Houses” walks from Pleasant Street⟦6⟧. Nearly every house is a private home: look from the sidewalk.
Walk: about 2 hours with stops. Drive: about 2 hours for stops 9–12.

In 1932 Milton Avery invited two young New York painters, Mark Rothko and Adolph Gottlieb, to Gloucester. They drew the bathers on the beaches and the wharfs across the harbor. Six stops, from the beach to the fish flakes.

The three painters’ summers here are the subject of ⟦0⟧Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea⟦1⟧, shown at the Cape Ann Museum in 2026⟦2⟧ and at the Phillips Collection in Washington from October 24, 2026, to January 24, 2027⟦3⟧. Rothko and Gottlieb rented cheap rooms and kept apart from the art colony’s social life, so few addresses survive⟦4⟧.
Half a day. Stops 3–5 are a short walk.

In August 2026 Christopher Rothko gave the museum his father’s ⟦0⟧Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts)⟦1⟧ of 1934, the first Rothko in its collection⟦2⟧. It shows the salt-fish sheds of the Reed and Gamage wharfs near Smith Cove, painted from Banner Hill (stop 5)⟦3⟧.

Avery painted the crowd watching the total solar eclipse of 1932 at Good Harbor⟦0⟧. Two years later the friends met here daily: Edith Rothko remembered that they would “go swimming and play handball,” and Rothko painted the game⟦1⟧. A sketch in his notebook shows the footbridge at Bass Rocks by Good Harbor Beach, a subject Leon Kroll had painted before him⟦2⟧.
On foot · about 0.5 km (0.5 mi) of streets

Avery first summered in Gloucester in 1921; in 1926 he and the sculptor Leonard Craske rented cottages here, the one record of where he stayed⟦0⟧. His ⟦1⟧Gloucester Dawn⟦2⟧ of about 1921 is at Vassar⟦3⟧.
The wharfs · Rocky Neck causeway · marker approximate

Smith Cove was the center of Gloucester’s gill-net fishing. Rothko painted its wharfs again and again in 1934: the Reed and Gamage salt-fish sheds with a water tank on the roof, and rows of fish flakes covered with white cloths to keep the sun off the fillets⟦0⟧; fishermen among the gill-net reels on a wharf⟦1⟧; and a schooner at a wharf with its sails lowered to dry, perhaps with City Hall on the skyline⟦2⟧.
The high view · above 186–220 East Main Street · marker approximate

The ridge above Smith Cove, where the Impressionists painted (site 3)⟦0⟧. Rothko painted the Reed and Gamage wharfs from Banner Hill, and Gottlieb sketched them from a similar spot, possibly beside him⟦1⟧. The hilltop is private; look from the road.
Rothko, summer 1934 · Calder Street, East Gloucester · marker approximate

In the summer of 1934 Rothko and his wife, Edith Sachar, rented a house on Calder Street, about half a mile from the wharfs, while the Averys and the Gottliebs summered nearby⟦0⟧. The Rothkos arrived first and took the house the Gottliebs had wanted⟦1⟧. The house number is not recorded; this is a quiet residential street.

Rothko’s Gloucester works on paper in public collections. Titles in brackets were supplied by the catalogue raisonné, which lists 38 works for Gloucester; the other 14 belong to the artist’s family⟦0⟧.
Back of the gill-net sheet; probably painted later

Rothko came back in 1945 and painted watercolors while staying with the photographer Aaron Siskind in East Gloucester, in the studio Gottlieb had found for Siskind the year before⟦0⟧. See ⟦1⟧the photographers⟦2⟧.
Some of Gottlieb’s Cape Ann pictures show dead fish he gathered on the beach and set in boxes⟦0⟧. His ⟦1⟧Harbor Scene⟦2⟧ of about 1934 is in the guide.
A sketchbook Avery used about 1943 is inscribed for the Mother Ann Cottage on Eastern Point; it is at the National Gallery of Art⟦0⟧.
